1. J Am Dent Assoc. 2026 May;157(5):471-486. doi: 10.1016/j.adaj.2026.02.010.
Epub  2026 Apr 6.

An update on community water fluoridation, part 2: Fluoride exposure and 
children's intelligence (IQ) scores-relevance of systematic reviews and 
meta-analyses to community water fluoridation.

Kumar JV(1), Levy SM(2), Warren JJ(3).

Author information:
(1)California Department of Public Health, Sacramento, CA; Now Retired, 
Clarksburg, MD. Electronic address: Jayvkumar@gmail.com.
(2)Department of Preventive and Community Dentistry, College of Public Health, 
University of Iowa, Iowa City, IA; Department of Epidemiology, College of Public 
Health, University of Iowa, Iowa City, IA.
(3)Graduate Program in Dental Public Health, The University of Iowa, Iowa City, 
IA.

BACKGROUND: The authors provide an overview of the literature on the association 
between fluoride (F) exposure related to community water fluoridation (CWF) and 
children's intelligence (IQ). It also critically evaluates the limitations of 
the evidence base.
TYPES OF STUDIES REVIEWED: This review is grounded in assessments from 4 
government reports and supplemented by means of 3 independent reports and 7 
other meta-analyses and systematic reviews. Collectively, these resources offer 
an overview of the literature on the relationship between F exposure and IQ. In 
addition, a meta-analysis of the association between urinary F and IQ is 
reanalyzed for its relevance to CWF.
RESULTS: The authors found there is no association between F concentrations 
relevant to CWF and IQ scores. Although researchers reported an association in 
endemic areas (ie, with F levels exceeding 1.5 mg/L), the design and conduct of 
these studies have numerous methodological weaknesses, including a limited 
number of high-quality studies; weak study designs; inadequate attention to 
accurately measuring F exposure, confounding variables, and outcomes; and the 
use of inappropriate statistical procedures. There is no established biological 
mechanism to explain F's effect on IQ. These limitations raise questions about 
the findings and preclude discussion of causal relationships. Furthermore, 
differences in water intake among countries should be considered when making 
cross-national comparisons.
CONCLUSIONS AND PRACTICAL IMPLICATIONS: The evidence does not support a causal 
link between F in drinking water and children's IQ. Dental and public health 
care practitioners should use this evidence to inform, educate, and empower 
patients and the public about the safety and benefits of CWF.
